Which of the following has been shown to be of prophylactic benefit in reducing the duration and severity of post 
operative delirium? 
 
Olanzapine 
 
Quetiapine 
 
Risperidone 
 
Haloperidol 
 
Chlorpromazine 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Haloperidol 
 
Haloperidol has been shown to reduce the severity and duration of post operative delirium in elderly patients undergoing hip 
surgery. Interestingly it did not recduce the incidence. 
Delirium (management) 
Pharmacological management of delirium 
Haloperidol has been shown to be of prophylactic use in delirium. 
NICE guidelines recommend short term haloperidol or olanzapine where delirium is associated with distress. 
 
Non-pharmacological management 
The following are recommended by NICE to assist in the management of delirium:- 
 Appropriate lighting and clear signage (use of calendars and a clock) 
 Talking to the person to reorientate them 
 Cognitively stimulating activities (e.g. reminiscence) 
 Regular visits from family and friends 
 Promote good sleep patterns 
Which SSRI was used as the level one treatment in the STAR*D study? 
 
Sertraline 
 
Citalopram 
 
Paroxetine 
 
Fluoxetine 
 
Fluvoxamine 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Citalopram 
 
STAR*D study 
The STAR*D trial (Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to relieve depression) was a pragmatic trail which aimed to assess the 
effectiveness of treatments in patients diagnosed with major depressive disorder. 
 
Method 
Patients were started on a treatment called level 1. If they failed to respond to this they were given another treatment called level 2. 
This continued up to level 4. 
 
Level 1 - This consisted of citalopram 
 
Level 2 - This consisted of either swapping to sertraline, Bupropion, or venlafaxine, or augmenting with Bupropion, or buspirone. 
Cognitive psychotherapy was also included as a switch or add on at this level. 
 
Level 3 - This consisted of swapping to mirtazapine or nortriptyline or adding on lithium or triiodothyronine (T3). 
 
Level 4 - This consisted of swapping to either tranylcypromine (MAOI) or a combination of venlafaxine and mirtazapine. 
Outcome measure used was remission (becoming symptom free). 
 
Main conclusions 
 In level 1 1/3 of participants achieved remission. A further 10-15% responded but not to the point of remission. 
 If treatment with an initial SSRI fails then 1 in 4 who choose to switch to another medication will enter remission regardless 
of whether the second medication is an SSRI or a medication of a different class. If patients choose instead to add a 
medication on 1 in 3 will get better. 
Which of the following tricyclic antidepressants is not recommended for use in breastfeeding women? 
 
Amitriptyline 
 
Doxepin 
 
Nortriptyline 
 
Imipramine 
 
Dosulepin 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Doxepin 
 
All tricyclic antidepressants, except doxepin, can safely be given to a woman who is breastfeeding provided the infant is full term, 
healthy and his or her progress is monitored. Poor sucking and swallowing, muscle hypotonia, drowsiness and vomiting were 
reported in a 9 day old breastfed infant whose mother was taking doxepin 35mg daily. 
Antenatal pharmacology 
For how long should a patient with a single episode of depression remain on an antidepressant? 
 
For 2 years in total 
 
For 6-9 months following complete remission 
 
For 12 months following the first sign of improvement 
 
For a minimum of 3 months following complete remission 
 
For 3 years from the beginning of the depressive episode 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : For 6-9 months following complete remission 
Depression (treatment duration) 
A single episode of depression should be treated for 6-9 months following complete remission. If antidepressants are stopped 
immediately on recovery, 50% of patients experience a relapse within 3-6 months. 
 
NICE recommend that patients who have had 2 or more depressive episodes (within recent history) should be treated with an 
antidepressant for a minimum of 2 years. 
 
Regarding migration as a risk factor for schizophrenia, which of the following is true? 
 
The relative risk for developing schizophrenia among second-generation migrants is 4.5 
 
Migrants from developing versus developed countries have a lower relative risk for the development of 
schizophrenia 
 
Migrants from areas where the majority of the population is black have a lower relative risk for the 
development of schizophrenia 
 
First generation migrants are at a higher risk of developing schizophrenia than second generation migrants 
 
Having experienced obstetric complications represents a greater risk of developing schizophrenia than being 
a migrant 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : The relative risk for developing schizophrenia among second-generation migrants is 4.5 
 
The relative risk for obstetric complications is approximately 2.0. 
Schizophrenia (migrant populations) 
Migration is a risk factor for the development of schizophrenia. 
In the most comprehensive review of this topic, the mean weighted relative risk for developing schizophrenia among first-generation 
migrants (40 effect sizes) was 2.7 (95% confidence interval [CI]= 2.3-3.2). 
A separate analysis performed for second-generation migrants (seven effect sizes) yielded a relative risk of 4.5 (95% CI=1.5-13.1). 
An analysis performed for studies concerning both first- and secondgeneration migrants and studies that did not distinguish 
between generations (50 effect sizes) yielded a relative risk of 2.9 (95% CI=2.5-3.4). 
Subgroup comparisons yielded significantly greater effect sizes for migrants from developing versus developed countries (relative 
risk=3.3, 95% CI=2.8-3.9) and for migrants from areas where the majority of the population is black (relative risk=4.8, 95% CI=3.7-
6.2) versus white and neither black nor white. 
In clinical trials of depression, what percentage reduction in depressive symptoms is generally considered to 
constitute a response to treatment? 
 
10% 
 
80% 
 
50% 
 
40% 
 
20% 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : 50% 
Antidepressants (effectiveness) 
IN clinical trials a 'response' is usually defined as a 50% reduction in depression rating scores. 
In patients with moderate depression the number needed to treat (NNT) for antidepressants over placebo is 5 and the NNT for 
antidepressants over true no-treatment is 3. 
A 68 year old man with a progressive history of breathlessness is taken to A&E by his wife. She tells the doctor that 
his breathing has recently become worse. He is diagnosed with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and started 
on a number of new medications. Two weeks later after starting these medications he returns to A&E, this time his 
wife complains that he has stopped sleeping, has become agitated, and will not stop talking. Which of the 
following is most likely to have caused his new presentation? 
 
Ipratropium 
 
Salbutamol 
 
Albuterol 
 
Budesonide 
 
Theophylline 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Budesonide 
 
Budesonide is an inhaled steroid. Inhaled steroids have been observed to precipitate hypomania and mania. 
Mania (drug induced) 
There is good evidence that mania can be precipitated by the following:- 
 Levodopa 
 Corticosteroids 
 Anabolic-androgenic steroids 
 Antidepressants (tricyclic and monoamine oxidase inhibitor classes) 
There is also evidence (albeit weaker) that mania can be precipitated by:- 
 Dopaminergic anti-Parkinsonian drugs 
 Thyroxine 
 Iproniazid and isoniazid 
 Chloroquine 
Which of the following drugs must not be used if a patient is taking clozapine? 
 
Sulpride 
 
Carbamazepine 
 
Lamotrigine 
 
Valproate 
 
Lorazepam 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Carbamazepine 
 
Carbamazepine is known to cause agranulocytosis so must be avoided. 
Sulpride and lamotrigine are useful augmentation agents for clozapine resistant schizophrenia. 
Valproate is used as a prophylaxis for seizures when using clozapine. 
Clozapine (neutropenia and agranulocytosis) 
Neutropenia refers to a decrease in circulating neutrophils. The term agranulocytosis is used to communicate a more severe subset 
of neutropenia. Agranulocytosis refers to a virtual absence of neutrophils in peripheral blood. 
 
Neutropenia 
Around 2.7% of patients treated with clozapine develop neutropenia. Of these, half do so within the first 18 weeks, and three-
quarters by the end of the first year (Maudsley, 2012). 
 
Risk factors for neutropenia include:- 
 Race (Afro-Caribbean 77% increase in risk) 
 Age (decrease in risk as age increases) 
 Low baseline white cell count 
Note: Risk is NOT dose related 
 
Agranulocytosis 
Agranulocytosis is defined as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of less than 0.5 * 10^9/L. It is estimated to occur in 0.8% of 
patients. It can be fatal if not detected early. 
With adequate monitoring the case fatality rate appears to be around 3% (of those who develop agranulocytosis 3% will die). 
Clozapine must not be used alongside other drugs known to cause agranulocytosis e.g. carbamazepine. 
Lithium has been shown to independently raise the white cell count and has been used in this way successfully in combination with 
clozapine. Use of this combination can enable patients to continue on treatment when they develop neutropenia. Having said that 
there are case reports suggesting that the combined use of lithium and clozapine can result in toxicity and so this combination must 
be used with caution. 
 
Risk factors for clozapine induced agranulocytosis include:- 
 Age (increasing age increases risk) 
 Ethnicity (Asians are 2.4 times more likely than Caucasians to develop agranulocytosis on clozapine) 
Note: the risk factors for neutropenia and agranulocytosis are quite different! 
 
Rechallenge 
One-third of patients who stop clozapine due to neutropenia or agranulocytosis will develop a blood dyscrasia on rechallenge. In 
most cases, the second reaction will occur more rapidly, be more severe, and will last longer than the first (Maudsley, 2012).  
 
Which of the following mood stabilizers has the best evidence to support its use as an augmentation option in 
clozapine resistant schizophrenia? 
Phenytoin 
 
Carbamazepine 
 
Lamotrigine 
 
Sodium valproate 
 
Topiramate 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Lamotrigine 
Clozapine (resistant schizophrenia) 
Treatment resistant schizophrenia has been estimated to be around 20%.  
Before concluding that a patient is clozapine resistant several factors need to be considered. 
 
Adequate duration of treatment. A substantial proportion of patients have a delayed response. 30% are expected to respond 
within 6 weeks, a further 20% by 3 months, and a further 20% by six months. 
 
Dosage. Plasma levels correlate poorly with clinical response. It is accepted however that a plasma level of 350-450ng/ml must be 
achieved before a patient can be considered resistant. As clozapine undergoes significant metabolism by the P450 enzymes, the 
effects of other medications and smoking need to be considered. 
 
Augmentation 
Should an adequate trial of clozapine fail to be of benefit, augmentation with additional antipsychotics or anti epileptics should be 
considered. 
Sulpride and amisulpride are the favoured antipsychotics for augmentation with clozapine as their selectivity for D2 dopamine 
blockade compliments clozapine (which lacks high potency dopamine blockade). 
Lamotrigine has the best evidence of the mood stabilisers to support its use as an augmentation strategy. 
 
The Maudsley guidelines list the following options for clozapine augmentation:- 
 Amisulpride 
 Aripiprazole 
 Haloperidol 
 Lamotrigine 
 Omega-3-triglycerides 
 Risperidone 
 Sulpiride 
 Topiramate 
 Ziprasidone 
They specifically suggest avoiding using the following:- 
 Pimozide 
 Olanzapine

Which of the following features is suggestive of mania rather than hypomania? 
 
Delusions of grandeur 
 
Decreased need for sleep

A 30 year old man experiences recurrent episodes of chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, and feelings of unreality, 
that occur suddenly without any obvious trigger and resolve spontaneously within 5-10 minutes. Which of the 
following is the most likely diagnosis? 
 
Panic disorder 
 
Personality disorder 
 
Social phobia 
 
Drug misuse 
 
Thyrotoxicosis 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Panic disorder 
 
The lack of trigger rules out a diagnosis of social phobia. The brevity of the episodes strongly suggests a diagnosis of panic 
disorder. 
Panic disorder 
Panic disorder is characterised by recurrent attacks of severe anxiety that are not restricted to any particular situation and so are 
unpredictable. Typical symptoms seen in panic attacks include the sudden onset of palpitations, breathlessness, chest pain, 
choking sensations, dizziness, depersonalisation, and derealisation. Attacks usually last for minutes only. 
NICE suggest SSRIs as first-line for panic disorder. If contraindicated or no response after 12 weeks then imipramine or 
clomipramine should be offered. 
 
Which of the following treatments is recommended by NICE for women with borderline personality disorder who 
recurrently self-harm? 
 
Cognitive analytic therapy 
 
Psychodynamic psychotherapy 
 
Dialectical behaviour therapy 
 
Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing 
 
Interpersonal therapy 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Dialectical behaviour therapy 
 
Exam Question Nov 2008 
 
The NICE guidelines on borderline personality disorder are quite vague when it comes to psychological treatment. They suggest 
that it should be tailored to the needs of the patient. 
They do suggest however that for women with BPD and recurrent self-harm dialectic behavioural therapy should be used. 
Personality disorder - borderline 
Features 
Features of borderline personality disorder include:- 
 Efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment 
 Unstable interpersonal relationships which alternate between idealization and devaluation 
 Unstable self image 
 Impulsivity in potentially self damaging area (e.g. Spending, sex, substance abuse) 
 Recurrent suicidal behaviour 
 Affective instability 
 Chronic feelings of emptiness 
 Difficulty controlling temper 
 Quasi psychotic thoughts 
Abuse 
Childhood abuse and neglect are extremely common among borderline patients. Up to 87% have suffered childhood trauma of 
some sort, 40-71% have been sexually abused and 25-71% have been physically abused (Winston, 2000). The effect of abuse 
seems to depend on the stage of psychological development at which it takes place. In general, the earlier it takes place, the more 
damaging it is likely to be. 
 
Co-morbidity 
In comparison to non-borderline PD patients, borderline PD patients more frequently received a diagnosis of current major 
depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar I and II disorder, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social and specific phobia, post-traumatic 
stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), eating disorder NOS, and any somatoform disorder (Zimmerman 
1999). 
Major depression is the most common with rates ranging from 53% to 83% (Bellino 2005).  
 
You are called to assess a man on a general medical ward who has been admitted due to a chest infection. The 
medical team are concerned that he may be depressed and have started him on treatment. You are concerned by 
his QTc interval which measures as 490 msec. Which of the following medications that he is prescribed would be 
most likely to be contributing to his prolonged QTc? 
 
Diazepam 
 
Paracetamol 
 
Simvastatin 
 
Erythromycin 
 
Sertraline 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Erythromycin 
 
QTc prolongation 
 
In addition to psychotropic drugs, there are a number of additional risk factors for QTc prolongation to consider. 
QTc prolongation is an indicator of risk of torsade de pointes and increased cardiac mortality. 
 
Risk factors for QTc prolongation 
Long QT syndrome 
Bradycardia 
Ischaemic heart disease 
Myocarditis 
Risk factors for QTc prolongation 
Myocardial infarction 
Left ventricular hypertrophy 
 
Hypokalaemia 
Hypomagnesaemia 
Hypocalcaemia 
 
Extreme physical exertion 
Stress or shock 
Anorexia nervosa 
Extremes of age (old or young) 
Female gender 
 
You should also be aware that a number of non-psychotopic drugs can cause QTc prolongation. 
 
Class Examples 
Antibiotics Ampicillin 
Erythromycin 
Antiarrthythmics Amiodarone 
Sotalol 
Antimalarials Chloroquine 
Quinine 
Others Methadone 
Tamoxifen 
Amantadine 
 
 
A patient with AIDS attends clinic in view of on-going depression. You note a number of cutaneous lesions in the 
form of purple-red macules on their face and neck. These are also apparent on the mucous membranes. Which of 
the following would you most suspect? 
 
Mycobacterium avium 
 
Kaposi's sarcoma 
 
Toxoplasma gondii 
 
Candidiasis 
 
Herpes simplex virus 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Kaposi's sarcoma 
 
Kaposi's sarcoma is a tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 . 
 
AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma typically presents with cutaneous lesions that begin as one or several red to purple-red macules, 
rapidly progressing to papules, nodules, and plaques, with a predilection for the head, back, neck, trunk, and mucous membranes. 
In more advanced cases, they can be found in the stomach and intestines, the lymph nodes, and the lungs. 
 
HIV 
 
The Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS) is a multi-system disorder that can have psychiatric manifestations. These may 
be due to infection as well as from its management. 
AIDS was first reported in the USA in 1981. In 1983 it was shown to be due to infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, 
HIV-1. This is a single-stranded retrovirus which is destructive of CD4 lymphocytes. The virus also destroys neuronal cells. 
 
Modes of transmission: 
 sexual 
 parenteral blood or blood product recipients 
 vertical from mother to child in utero 
 
Clinical presentation 
 
Main clinical manifestations: 
 candidiasis 
 cryptococcus 
 cryptosporidiosis 
 cytomegalovirus 
 herpes simplex virus 
 Kaposi's sarcoma 
 mycobacterium avium 
 mycobacterium tuberculosis 
 pneumocystis jiroveci (formally known as pneumocyctis carinii) 
 toxoplasma gondii 
 
Approximately two to four weeks after infection, the majority of patients develop a flu-like syndrome, characterised by: 
 a self-limiting fever 
 fatigue 
 rash 
 pharyngitis with cervical adenitis 
 arthralgia 
 myalgia 
 
Following initial infection, there is usually an asymptomatic period before the onset of the various opportunistic infections 
 
Diagnosis 
 
Diagnosis is based on the detection of the P24 antigen, HIV nucleic acid or direct virus detection. Antibodies are detectable within 
about six weeks of infection and persist for life. 
Severity of disease and response to treatment are monitored by measuring the CD4 count and viral load. Decreases in CD4 counts 
correlate with opportunistic infections. 
Most individuals are asymptomatic when their CD4 counts are >500 x 10^6/l. They are at greatest risk when this count falls below 
200 x 10^6/l. 
 
Antiretroviral drugs 
These are not curative but are effective in reducing viral loads and increasing CD4 counts. 
The following table illustrates the classification of antiretrovirals: 
 
Class Examples

nevirapine 
Nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors abacavir 
didanosine

indinavir 
Others enfuvirtide

and is most likely to appear in the exam. 
 
Co-morbidity and prescribing 
Affective and anxiety syndromes are the commonest conditions; manic and psychotic disorders are less frequent. Most psychiatric 
conditions can co-occur. 
The following table lists the suggestions by the Maudsley Guidelines in cases of HIV. 
 
Problem Suggestions 
Psychosis Atypicals are suggested. Risperidone is the most widely studied 
Delirium Atypicals and low-dose short acting benzodiazepines

Bipolar Valproate, lamotrigine, gabapentin are the best options, lithium ok but poorly tolerated.

Agomelatine seems not to cause sexual adverse effects.

The characteristic rash seen in Lyme disease is called erythema migrans. It usually tack the appearance of a circular, outwardly

Lyme disease 
Lyme disease is an infectious disease cause by a tick bite. It usually presents with fatigue, fever, malaise, and a skin rash known as 
erythema migrans. If untreated it can lead to problems with the heart, joints, and CNS. 
 
Which of the following is true regarding clozapine? 
 
 Clozapine binds tightly to D2 receptors 
 Clozapine induces catalepsy in animal models 
A history of clozapine induced agranulocytosis is an absolute contraindication for further clozapine use 
 N-desmethylclozapine is a major metabolite of clozapine

N-desmethylclozapine is a major metabolite of clozapine 
A history of clozapine induced agranulocytosis is a relative (not absolute) contraindication for further clozapine use. In some 
circumstances where the need for clozapine is pronounced therapy can be re-initiated under close monitoring with the possible 
provision of the hormone G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). 
Clozapine binds loosely (not tightly) to D2 receptors (hence the reduce potential for movement disorders). It also binds to D1, D3, 
D4, and D5 receptors. 
Clozapine does not induce catalepsy in animal models (unlike most antipsychotics). catalepsy is indicated by rigidity, inactivity, 
reduced pain response, and the slowing of bodily functions such as breathing). 
CYP1A2 (not CYP2D6) is primarily responsible for the metabolism of clozapine.

Bipolar disorder (Rapid cycling) 
 
Rapid cycling is defined as 4 or more mood episodes per year. It has an estimated prevalence of 10-20% of all patients with bipolar 
disorder (estimated from specialised western mood disorder clinics). It tends to develop late in the course of the disorder and lasts 
less than 2 years in 50% of patients. It is associated with an increased risk of suicide. 
Compared with non-rapid-cycling bipolar disorder, it is:- 
 More common in women 
 Associated with an earlier age at onset 
 Associated with a greater illness burden 
 Associated with higher treatment resistance

The AESOP study found the lowest incidence rates for psychosis in which of the following groups? 
 
Asian 
 
African-Caribbean 
 
White British 
 
Other 
 
Black African 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : White British 
The AESOP study 
The AESOP (Aetiology and Ethnicity of Schizophrenia and Other Psychoses) study is a large first-presentation study of 
schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. Over 2 years, this 3 centre study identified all people presenting to services with 
psychotic symptoms in well-defined catchment areas in South London, Nottingham and Bristol.  
Comprehensive biological, social, demographic and neuropsychological information was obtained by interview with both the 
individuals and their carers. In addition, over 100 individuals in the study had a structural MRI brain scan. 
The overall aims of the study are threefold: firstly, to elucidate the overall rates of psychotic disorder in the 3 centres; secondly, to 
confirm and extend previous findings of raised rates of psychosis in certain migrant groups in the UK; and finally, to explore in detail 
the biological and social risk factors in these populations and their possible interactions. 
 
Main findings 
The incidence of all psychoses was found to be higher in African-Caribbean and Black African populations. These differences were 
most marked in schizophrenia and manic psychosis. After adjusting for age the incidence of schizophrenia was 9 times higher in 
African-Caribbean and 6 times higher in Black African compared to the White British group. The incidence rates for all ethnic 
minority groups were raised compared to the White British group albeit less markedly. 
African-Caribbean and Black African patients were more likely to be compulsorily admitted to hospital. The same groups were more 
likely to come to the attention of mental health services via police or other criminal justice agencies, and less likely to come via the 
GP.

Clozapine has a complex pharmacology. It has antagonistic activity at the D1, D2, D3 and D4 dopamine receptors, alpha-1 and 
alpha-2 adrenergic, 5-HT2 serotonin, H1 histamine and M1, M2, M3 and M5 receptors, with agonist activity at the M4 muscarinic 
receptor.  
Hypersalivation is a paradoxical side-effect because clozapine has marked anticholinergic properties. Parasympathetic stimulation 
causes high salivary flow rates and sympathetic stimulation leads to high protein levels. The agonist effect of clozapine on the 
muscarinic M4 receptor has been put forward to explain in part the paradoxical hypersalivation. Another proposed mechanism is 
clozapine's antagonist activity at the alpha-2 adrenoceptor. While muscarinic blockade leads to diminished salivary secretion, alpha-
2 antagonists can increase salivation. An additional mechanism that has been proposed is that clozapine reduces the frequency of 
swallowing.

Schizophrenia (Crow) 
Crow proposed a categorical model of schizophrenia and divided patients into types I and II. 
Type I patients present with positive symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. Crow proposed that the underlying 
mechanism for this subtype was a biochemical imbalance, such as an excess of dopamine D2 receptors. He hypothesized that 
these patients would respond more favourably to antipsychotic medication. 
Patients with type II schizophrenia present with negative symptoms such as affective flattening and poverty of speech. He 
suggested that these patients have an underlying structural/anatomical abnormality such as ventricular enlargement or cortical 
atrophy. Patients with type II tend respond poorly to treatment, follow a chronic course, and have a poor outcome.

Approximately what percentage of patients who attend hospital with self-harm receive a psychosocial 
assessment from a mental health practitioner? 
 
70% 
 
10% 
 
30% 
 
90% 
 
50% 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : 50% 
 
Approximately half the patients who attend hospital having self harmed actually receive a psychosocial assessment (from either a 
psychiatrist or allied health professional). There is also some evidence to suggest that the half that is seen may be the lower risk 
group. 
Self-harm 
Self-harm refers to any act of self-poisoning or self-injury (this does not include drinking too much alcohol, or accidental self-harm). 
Self-harm is common among younger people. A survey of young people aged 15-16 years estimated that more than 10% of girls 
and more than 3% of boys had self-harmed in the previous year. For all age groups, annual prevalence is approximately 0.5%. 
One systematic review (Owens, 2002) reported that a median of 16% of self-harm patients repeat within one year. 
People who attend an emergency department after an incident of self-harm will often have visited their GP in the previous month 
(approximately half). 
Risk assessment tools and scales 
Risk assessment tools are described by NICE as 'crude'. They are NOT recommended for: 
 Predicting future suicide or repetition of self-harm 
 Determining who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged 
Interventions for self-harm 
NICE recommend: 
 3 to 12 sessions of a psychological intervention that is specifically structured for people who self-harm 
 Drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm should not be offered 
General management of ingestion 
Activated charcoal can help if used early (within 2 hours of ingestion). It should only be used for drugs where it is expected to be 
effective in reducing absorption. The patient needs to be fully conscious and able to protect their own airway. 
Emetics, including ipecac (ipecacuanha), should not be used in the 
management of self-poisoning. 
Cathartics as a specific treatment should not be used in the management of 
self-poisoning. 
Gastric lavage should generally not be used unless recommended by TOXBASE. 
 
Paracetamol 
Paracetamol is involved in between 30 and 40% of acute presentations with poisoning.  
It is is toxic to the liver as a result of conversion to a benzoquinonimine metabolite which is normally conjugated with the amino acid 
glutathione. The metabolism of paracetamol via this route is inducible, and therefore more rapid in patients on inducing drugs (e.g. 
phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates, rifampicin, St John's Wort) or who are chronic alcoholics. Alcoholics who have recently 
stopped drinking are at greatest risk. Supplies of glutathione in the liver depend on the patient's diet and there is suspicion that 
acute starvation may therefore represent an additional risk factor to the known ones of eating disorders and chronic malnutrition. 
Levels should be measured for risk assessment no earlier than 4 hours and no later than 15 hours after ingestion. Intravenous 
acetylcysteine is the treatment of choice. 
Treatment is generally divided into four phases:- 
 1 - Before four hours have elapsed after ingestion, blood levels are not interpretable. It is unnecessary and inappropriate to 
administer acetylcysteine. 
 2 - Between four and eight hours after exposure there is time to obtain a plasma concentration to decide if treatment is 
necessary. 
 3 - After eight hours. Only after this time should 'blind' treatment with acetylcysteine be commenced, and only then if the 
patient has ingested more than a potentially toxic amount: >150 mg/kg in a normal patient, less in an 'at risk' patient. 
Treatment can be stopped if the paracetamol level is below threshold. 
 4 - Beyond 24 hours. Acetylcysteine is most effective when given early in preventing liver damage. Its effect declines from 
about 12 hours and management approaches therefore change for presentations 24 hours or more after ingestion. 
Acetylcysteine is used at this time to treat acute liver failure, and not act as a specific paracetamol antidote. In patients 
who present late, it is reasonable to obtain blood results and determine treatment based on these. Samples should include 
liver function tests (ALT or AST (alanine or aspartate aminotransferase)), prothrombin time, serum electrolytes, and a 
paracetamol level, which may be undetectable even in severe liver failure. 
Acetylcysteine is normally administered for 20 hours. Pseudo-allergic reactions are relatively common (5-10%) and should be 
treated with antihistamines. A larger proportion of patients (approx 25%) suffer nausea or vomiting. True anaphylaxis has not been 
observed and a history of previous reactions is not a reason not to treat. 
A small proportion of patients develop renal damage from paracetamol, in the absence of any major liver damage. Renal damage is 
a common complication of acute liver failure and an important index of its severity. 
 
Opiates 
Opioids are commonly prescribed for treating chronic pain and are often misused and abused to achieve euphoria. Opioid 
overdoses can result in life-threatening effects such as respiratory depression, hypoxia, coma, bradycardia, 
hypotension/hypertension, and CNS depression. 
Naloxone is used as an antidote for opioid overdose. It is a pure opioid competitive antagonist at all receptor sites (mu, kappa, and 
delta). Naloxone reverses coma and respiratory depression from all opioids, including partial agonists such as buprenorphine, 
without adding any agonist effects (respiratory depression, sedation, analgesia, miosis). 
 
Benzodiazepines 
Flumazenil, can help reduce the need for admission to intensive care. Although widely used, flumazenil is not currently licensed for 
the treatment of benzodiazepine overdose in the UK. 
Flumazenil should be avoided in patients who may have ingested proconvulsants, (tricyclic antidepressants), those with a history of 
epilepsy, and patients who are dependent upon benzodiazepines. 
 
Skin lacerations 
For superficial uncomplicated injuries of 5 cm or less in length, the use of tissue adhesive should be offered as a first-line treatment 
option. Skin closure strips could be used instead if the patient prefers. 
 
Children 
All children who self-harm should be admitted for an overnight stay at a paediatric ward.

Which of the following commonest method of suicide in the England? 
 
Suffocation 
 
Poisoning by overdose 
 
Carbon monoxide poisoning 
 
Hanging 
 
Drowning

Suicide and homicide 
 
Key findings from the National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Homicide by people with mental illness, taken from 
the 2014 report. 
 
Suicide general 
The report recorded an average suicide rate of approximately 1 per 10,000 in the general population. This figure is pretty stable 
over the years so is certainly one worth remembering. 
It is more common in males than females (3:1). 
 
Methods of suicide 
In the general population the most common methods of suicide tend to be (in descending order):- 
 Hanging/strangulation 
 Self-poisoning 
 Jumping and multiple injuries (mainly jumping from a height or being struck by a train) 
 CO poisoning and drowning (these occur at approximately the same rate) 
 Cutting and stabbing 
Note: The methods used in mental health patients are roughly similar. 
 
Patient suicide 
During 2002-2012, 28% of general population suicides were identified as patient suicides, i.e. the person had been in contact with 
mental health services in the 12 months prior to death. 10% of patient suicides occurred as in-patients. 
The suicide rate for mental health users is around 1 in 1000 (10 times higher than general population). 
Opiates were the most common type of drug in self-poisoning (23%). 
The first 3 months after discharge remain a time of particularly high suicide risk. Between 2002-12, 18% of all patient suicides 
occurred within 3 months.  
 
Information from the Office of National Statistics 2014 
Suicide tends to be highest in the 40-44 age group. 
The two most common methods of suicide among men in the United Kingdom are hanging, strangulation and suffocation, followed 
by poisoning. The reverse is true among women: the most common method of suicide is poisoning, followed by hanging, 
strangulation and suffocation. 
 
Key findings from the National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Homicide by people with mental illness, taken from 
the 2014 report. 
 
General Homicide 
The most common method of homicide was the use of a sharp instrument (40%). 
The relationship of victim to offender was: acquaintance (42%), stranger (26%) spouse/partner (current/ex) (20%), and other family 
member (12%). 
About 6% of all perpetrators of homicide in England had a history of schizophrenia. Of these, 79% had symptoms of psychosis 
(delusions and/or hallucinations) at the time of the offence. 
 
Mental illness at time of homicide 
Around 10% of people convicted of homicide in England are considered to have an abnormal mental state at the time of the 
offence. 
Mentally ill perpetrators are less likely to kill a stranger than those without mental illness. 
 
Homicides by people involved with mental health services 
10% of the total sample of homicides were confirmed as patients, i.e. the person had been in contact with mental health services in 
the 12 months prior to the offence. 
Of the patients, the relationship of victim to offender was: acquaintance (42%), spouse/partner (current/ex) (21%), and family 
member (21%). 17% were stranger homicides.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a chronic type of communicating hydrocephalus (an abnormal accumulation of CSF in the 
ventricles of the brain). It is thought to be due to the impaired reabsorption of CSF by the arachanoid villi. The CSF pressure is 
typically high but still within the normal range, for this reason it does not present with features of high ICP such as headache and 
nausea. Instead patients tend to present with the classic triad of incontinence, gait ataxia, and dementia (wet, wobbly, wacky). For 
this reason it is often misdiagnosed as Parkinson's, and Alzheimer's. 
 
The AESOP study found the highest incidence rates for psychosis in which of the following groups? 
 
Black African 
 
White British 
 
Asian 
 
African-Caribbean 
 
Other

The AESOP study 
The AESOP (Aetiology and Ethnicity of Schizophrenia and Other Psychoses) study is a large first-presentation study of 
schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders. Over 2 years, this 3 centre study identified all people presenting to services with 
psychotic symptoms in well-defined catchment areas in South London, Nottingham and Bristol.  
Comprehensive biological, social, demographic and neuropsychological information was obtained by interview with both the 
individuals and their carers. In addition, over 100 individuals in the study had a structural MRI brain scan. 
The overall aims of the study are threefold: firstly, to elucidate the overall rates of psychotic disorder in the 3 centres; secondly, to 
confirm and extend previous findings of raised rates of psychosis in certain migrant groups in the UK; and finally, to explore in detail 
the biological and social risk factors in these populations and their possible interactions. 
 
Main findings 
The incidence of all psychoses was found to be higher in African-Caribbean and Black African populations. These differences were 
most marked in schizophrenia and manic psychosis. After adjusting for age the incidence of schizophrenia was 9 times higher in 
African-Caribbean and 6 times higher in Black African compared to the White British group. The incidence rates for all ethnic 
minority groups were raised compared to the White British group albeit less markedly. 
African-Caribbean and Black African patients were more likely to be compulsorily admitted to hospital. The same groups were more 
likely to come to the attention of mental health services via police or other criminal justice agencies, and less likely to come via the 
GP.

Which of the following was the first fully structured instrument developed to be used by lay interviewers? 
 
CIDI-R 
 
SCID 
 
CIDI 
 
DIS

CORRECT ANSWER : DIS 
 
Key epidemiological surveys 
Prior to 1980 it was difficult to perform any large epidemiological studies. This was due to a lack of any sophisticated measure to 
assess mental disorders. The only options were screening tools or expensive clinician administrated diagnostic interviews.  
Then along came the Diagnostic Interview Schedule (DIS) (Robins et al. 1981). This was the first fully structured diagnostic 
interview designed for use by lay interviewers. Seeing the potential the National Institute of Mental Health launched the 
Epidemiological Catchment Area (ECA) Programme. 
There was a problem though as many countries used ICD classification. For this reason the WHO developed a version of the DIS 
that used ICD criteria, which was called the WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI). 
The first large scale national survey to use the CIDI was the National Comorbidity Survey (NCS). The NCS took place in the early 
1990's. It improved on the ECA as it was a national survey. 
Both the ECA and the NCS suggested that the number of people with mental health problems far outnumbered to resources 
available. It was suggested that the data from the ECA and NCS overstated the demand as many of the cases of mental health 
were likely to be mild. The data from the ECA and NCS could not resolve this issue as they did not comment on severity. This led to 
the development of a revised version of the CIDI called the World Mental Health CIDI (WMH-CIDI), and the beginning of the WHO 
world mental health surveys. In addition to the issue of severity the WMH-CIDI also assesses a variety of other aspects of a 
disorder such as risk factors, socio-demographics, and treatments.

Exam Question Aug 2010 
 
Atypical anorexia is the term used to describe a presentation that does not quite meet the full diagnostic criteria for anorexia. E.g. A 
lady who is very thin, starving herself, has disturbed body image, but is still having normal periods. 
Anorexia (diagnosis) 
The DSM-IV provides the best guide to the diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. 
 
Diagnostic features include:- 
 Refusal to maintain body weight above 85% of what is expected 
 Intense fear of becoming fat despite being thin 
 Disturbed body image and denial of seriousness of there low body weight 
 Amenorrhea 
The type of anorexia must then be specified as either restrictive or purging. 
 Restrictive type (does not binge or purge) 
 Purging/ binging type (either engages in self induced vomiting or purges with laxatives, enemas, or diuretics) 
The term 'atypical anorexia nervosa' is used to describe cases in which patients present with a number of symptoms of anorexia 
that do not completely fulfill the diagnostic criteria for typical anorexia nervosa.

year using the Diagnostic Interview Schedule (DIS). 
Unfortunately the DIS diagnosis of schizophrenia was not congruent with psychiatrists' classification. For example in the Baltimore 
ECA site, the DIS identified only 20% of the cases of schizophrenia that the psychiatrist diagnosed on independent examination.

CORRECT ANSWER : Lithium has been shown to be an effective augmentation agent for people with unipolar

Lithium (evidence and indications) 
Although effective as a treatment for mania, lithium is rarely used for this as it takes up to a week to achieve a response. 
It is effective as a prophylactic agent for bipolar disorder where it reduces both the severity and number of relapses. It is more 
effective at preventing manic relapse rather than depressive. It also offers some protection against antidepressant induced 
hypomania. 
Lithium has also been shown to be effective as an augmentation agent in unipolar depression.

The borderline syndrome is characterised by which of the following? 
 
Affective stablity 
 
Consistent self image 
 
Quasi psychotic thoughts 
 
Euphoric affect 
 
Good impulse control 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Quasi psychotic thoughts 
Personality disorder – borderline 
Features 
Features of borderline personality disorder include:- 
 Efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment 
 Unstable interpersonal relationships which alternate between idealization and devaluation 
 Unstable self image 
 Impulsivity in potentially self damaging area (e.g. Spending, sex, substance abuse) 
 Recurrent suicidal behaviour 
 Affective instability 
 Chronic feelings of emptiness 
 Difficulty controlling temper 
 Quasi psychotic thoughts 
Abuse 
Childhood abuse and neglect are extremely common among borderline patients. Up to 87% have suffered childhood trauma of 
some sort, 40-71% have been sexually abused and 25-71% have been physically abused (Winston, 2000). The effect of abuse 
seems to depend on the stage of psychological development at which it takes place. In general, the earlier it takes place, the more 
damaging it is likely to be. 
 
Co-morbidity 
In comparison to non-borderline PD patients, borderline PD patients more frequently received a diagnosis of current major 
depressive disorder (MDD), bipolar I and II disorder, panic disorder with agoraphobia, social and specific phobia, post-traumatic 
stress disorder (PTSD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), eating disorder NOS, and any somatoform disorder (Zimmerman 
1999). 
Major depression is the most common with rates ranging from 53% to 83% (Bellino 2005).

A 55 year old lady with breast cancer taking Tamoxifen goes to see her GP with depression. The GP prescribes an 
antidepressant. Which of the following should the GP avoid in view of its interaction with Tamoxifen? 
 
Trazodone 
 
Amitriptyline 
 
Fluoxetine 
 
Moclobemide 
 
Mirtazapine 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Fluoxetine 
 
Exam Question Sep 2011 
Exam Question Oct 2010 
Tamoxifen 
Tamoxifen is a SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator) used for the treatment of breast cancer. It reduces relapse rates of 
breast cancer and increases overall survival.  
Tamoxifen's effects in the breast depend on its ability to antagonize oestrogen. Tamoxifen's anti-oestrogen affinity is thought to 
depend on the activity of its primary metabolite, endoxifen. Tamoxifen is metabolised to endoxifen through the liver enzyme 
CYP2D6. Consequently, any drug that inhibits this enzyme will reduce the conversion of tamoxifen to endoxifen. 
Women taking tamoxifen for the treatment or prevention of recurrence of breast cancer are likely to take antidepressants either for a 
psychiatric disorder or for hot flushes. Evidence suggests that some antidepressants inhibit the metabolism of tamoxifen to its more 
active metabolites by the cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) enzyme, thereby decreasing the anticancer effect. Based on current 
research, the psychotropic medications which are the strongest CYP2D6 inhibitors (and therefore most likely to interact) include 
paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion, duloxetine, while sertraline, escitalopram, and doxepin are moderate inhibitors, and venlafaxine is 
a weak inhibitor. 
 
A patient complains of hearing voices on a daily basis and has several delusional beliefs, in addition there signs of 
avolition. These symptoms have been present for 5 weeks. Prior to this the patient had a two month history of 
anxiety and increased social isolation. Select the most appropriate DSM-IV diagnosis 
 
Persistent delusional disorder 
 
Brief psychotic disorder 
 
Acute and transient psychotic disorder 
 
Schizophreniform disorder 
 
Schizophrenia 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Schizophreniform disorder 
 
The 5 week history of hallucination and delusions satisfies the DSM-IV requirement of 1 month of 'active symptoms'. The additional 
symptoms suggest a prodromal phase but for a diagnosis of schizophrenia the total duration of symptoms is 6 months. 
The term schizophreniform disorder plugs the gap between brief psychotic disorder' and schizophrenia. 
Schizophrenia (diagnosis, ICD-10 versus DSM-IV) 
Broadly speaking the DSM-IV and ICD-10 have a similar diagnostic approach to schizophrenia. They do however differ in the 
following ways. 
 
Symptom duration 
To meet a diagnosis of schizophrenia, the ICD-10 requires that symptoms of schizophrenia be present for at least one month. 
The DSM-IV requires symptoms to be present for at least 6 months, with at least a one month period of active symptoms.  
This difference reflects the fact that the DSM-IV recognises the prodromal phase of schizophrenia. 
A period of schizophrenic symptoms lasting less than one month is classified in the ICD-10 as an acute and transient psychotic 
disorder and in the DSM-IV as a brief psychotic episode. If a patient has had symptoms more than 1 month but less than 6 months 
then the term 'schizophreniform disorder' is used by the DSM-IV (prodromal phase). 
 
Social and occupational dysfunction 
The DSM-IV requires some impairment of social and occupational dysfunction. This is not a requirement of the ICD-10. 
Which of the following is true regarding hypnotics? 
 
Zopiclone is more likely to impair driving than benzodiazepines 
 
Younger people are more likely to experience adverse effects from hypnotics than the elderly 
 
Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics such as zolpidem are more effective in the treatment of insomnia than 
benzodiazepines 
 
Temazepam is not licensed for the treatment of insomnia 
 
Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics such as zolpidem are less likely to cause dependence than benzodiazepines 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Zopiclone is more likely to impair driving than benzodiazepines 
 
The Z drugs (zopiclone, zolpidem etc) were well marketed and for a while people believed they were more effective than the 
benzodiazepines and were less likely to produce dependence. This has not proved to be the case. 
Having said, some differences have been found. Zopiclone has been found to impair driving more than the benzodiazepines. 
NICE concluded that there was no difference in efficacy and that patients who fail to respond to a benzodiazepine should not be 
offered a non-benzodiazepine alternative (and vice versa). 
Insomnia (treatments) 
The NICE (2015) Clinical Knowledge Summary provides a useful guide on the management of insomnia. It splits the management 
into that of short-term insomnia (<4 weeks) and long-term insomnia (>4 weeks). 
 
Short-term insomnia: 
Consider a short course of a hypnotic drug only if daytime impairment is severe. 
The hypnotics recommended for the treatment of insomnia are: 
 Short-acting benzodiazepines temazepam, loprazolam, lormetazepam. 
 Non-benzodiazepines (the 'z-drugs') zopiclone, zolpidem, and zaleplon (all are short acting). 
 Diazepam is not generally recommended, but it can be useful if insomnia is associated with daytime anxiety 
If a hypnotic is prescribed: 
 Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period possible. The exact duration will depend on the underlying cause, but 
treatment should not continue for longer than 2 weeks. 
 Inform the person that further prescriptions for hypnotics will not usually be given, ensure that the reasons for this are 
understood, and document this in the person's notes. 
 Do not issue further prescriptions without seeing the person again. 
 If there has been no response to the first hypnotic, do not prescribe another. 
 If the person experiences adverse effects considered to be directly related to an hypnotic, consider switching to another 
hypnotic. 
Long-term insomnia 
Refer to psychological services for a cognitive or behavioural intervention. 
Pharmacological therapy is generally not recommended for the long-term management of insomnia but may be considered for 
immediate relief of symptoms. 
If prescribing medication, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period possible. The exact duration will depend on the 
underlying cause but should not continue for longer than 2 weeks. Up to 4 weeks' use may occasionally be required, but continued 
use should always be re-assessed after 2 weeks. 
For people over 55 years of age with persistent insomnia, consider treatment with a modified-release melatonin. The recommended 
initial duration of treatment is 3 weeks. If there is a response to treatment, it can be continued for a further 10 weeks. 
 
Additional detail from NICE regarding evidence base: 
There is insufficient evidence to assess the effectiveness of sleep hygiene as a single intervention; however its use is widely 
supported by expert opinion in current literature and guidelines.  
There is good evidence for the efficacy of hypnotic drugs in short-term insomnia; however, their use is associated with adverse 
effects. 
Tolerance to the hypnotic effects of benzodiazepine may be rapid, and may occur within a few days or weeks of regular use. 
Dependence is more likely to develop with long-term use, high doses, more potent or shorter-acting benzodiazepines, and a history 
of anxiety problems.  
Diazepam, nitrazepam, and flurazepam are not recommended because their long half-life commonly gives rise to next-day residual 
effects, and repeated doses tend to be cumulative. 
Sedative drugs other than hypnotics (such as antidepressants, antihistamines, choral hydrate, clomethiazole, and barbiturates) are 
not recommended for the management of insomnia. Expert opinion from reviews suggests that there is insufficient evidence to 
support their use, and that the potential for adverse effects is significant. 
 
Modified-release melatonin (Circadin®) is only licensed for the management of primary insomnia (usually defined as more than 4 
weeks' duration), and has only been studied in people with long-term insomnia. 
The evidence on the efficacy of acupuncture is generally of poor methodological quality with inconsistent results. There is some 
evidence from single studies in a Cochrane systematic review to suggest that acupuncture and its variants (acupressure and 
transcutaneous electrical stimulation) may improve quality of sleep. Results for other sleep variables were inconsistent. 
There is insufficient good quality evidence to make a recommendation regarding the efficacy of valerian, or any other herbal 
remedies, in the management of insomnia. 
 
Good sleep hygiene includes: 
 Establish fixed times for going to bed and waking up (and avoid sleeping in after a poor night's sleep). 
 Try to relax before going to bed. 
 Maintain a comfortable sleeping environment: not too hot, cold, noisy, or bright. 
 Avoid napping during the day. 
 Avoid caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol within 6 hours of going to bed. (Consider complete elimination of caffeine from the 
diet.) 
 Avoid exercise within 4 hours of bedtime (although exercise earlier in the day is beneficial). 
 Avoid eating a heavy meal late at night. 
 Avoid watching or checking the clock throughout the night. 
 Only use the bedroom for sleep and sexual activity.

Benzodiazepines appear to be associated with oral clefts in newborns and floppy baby syndrome. 
Olanzapine is recommended by the Maudsley guidelines in the situation of a pregnant patient in need of an antipsychotic. 
Paroxetine is more commonly associated with neonatal withdrawal than other SSRIs, it is also associated with an increased risk of 
congenital malformations compared with other antidepressants (Thormahelen 2006) 
The following table shows the current Maudsley guidelines on prescribing in pregnancy and breastfeeding. 
 
Drug class Suggested in pregnancy Suggested in breastfeeding 
Antidepressants Fluoxetine, amitriptyline, imipramine, (avoid paroxetine) Sertraline, paroxetine 
Antipsychotics Olanzapine, haloperidol, clozapine, chlorpromazine Olanzapine, sulpride 
Mood stabilisers Avoid if possible Avoid if possible and use antipsychotics 
instead. Valproate is recommended if 
essential 
Sedatives Promethazine For anxiety - Lorazepam 
For insomnia - Zolpidem 
 
 
Which of the following is not a recognised side effect of valproate? 
 
Weight loss 
 
Hair loss 
 
Tremor 
 
Nausea 
 
Lethargy 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Weight loss 
 
Main side effects of valproate:- 
 
 Nausea 
 Lethargy 
 Weight gain 
 Hair loss (with curly regrowth) 
 Tremor 
 
Weight gain is a significant problem with valproate especially is used with other drugs such as clozapine. 
Valproate 
NICE recommends valproate as a first-line option for the treatment of people who develop acute mania. 
Valproate is available in the following three forms:- 
 Semi-sodium valproate (licensed for acute mania associated with bipolar disorder) 
 Valproic acid (licensed for acute mania associated with bipolar disorder) 
 Sodium valproate (licensed for epilepsy) 
This gets a bit confusing as semi-sodium valproate (aka Depakote) is actually an equimolar mix of sodium valproate and valproic 
acid. 
Note this is from the BNF 61 and is not consistent with the Maudsley Guidelines 10th Edition which suggest valproic acid is not 
licensed for acute mania. 
Be aware that doses of sodium valproate and semi sodium valproate are not the same. A slightly higher dose (approx 10%) is 
required if sodium valproate is used. This is due o the fact that valproate semi-sodium 500 mg tablets contain 15.5% more valproic 
acid equivalent than sodium valproate 500 mg tablets. 
 
Adverse effects 
Valproate is associated with many adverse effects the most important ones to be aware of include:- 
 Tiredness (This is a common side effect that can present with slowing of mental processing speed and less motivation and 
less spontaneity) 
 Significant weight gain (weight gain affects 30% to 50% of people who take valproate) 
 Tremor (up to a quarter of patients) 
 Hair loss (hair loss occurs in 5% to 10% of people who take valproate. The hair almost always grows back after the 
valproate is stopped, but it often has a different texture and may grow in curly instead of straight) 
Teratogenic effects 
Valproate is a teratogen and so should not be initiated in women of childbearing potential.

Which of the following is the closest estimate of the incidence of puerperal psychosis? 
 
1 in 10000 
 
5 in 10000 
 
2 in 100 
 
1 in 10 
 
2 in 1000 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : 2 in 1000 
 
Puerperal psychosis incidence = 1-2 in 1000 
Exam Question Oct 2015 
Puerperal psychosis 
Postpartum psychosis should be thought of as a type of bipolar disorder (it is coded as a subtype of bipolar disorder in the DSM-V) 
The incidence is around 1-2 in 1000 pregnancies. 
The onset is usually rapid and occurs between day 2 and day 14 following delivery. Almost all cases occur within 8 weeks of 
delivery. 
Factors that increase the risk of puerperal psychosis include (Schopf 1994): 
 A past history of puerperal psychosis, pre-existing psychotic illness (especially affective psychosis) of severity requiring 
admission to hospital 
 A family history of affective psychosis in first or second degree relatives 
Factors shown not to be associated include (Jones 2001): 
 Twin pregnancy 
 Breast feeding 
 Single parenthood 
 Stillbirth 
Treatment 
Treatment is as per psychosis in general but one needs to consider the potential issues if the mother is breastfeeding. 
 
Which of the following is not recommended for people suffering with insomnia? 
 
Use bed only for sleeping 
 
Decrease alcohol intake 
 
Get regular exercise in the evening 
 
Use anxiety management and relaxation techniques 
 
Do not sleep during the day 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Get regular exercise in the evening 
Insomnia (sleep hygiene) 
Sleep hygiene must be attempted before medications are used to treat insomnia. 
Sleep hygiene approaches include:- 
 Increase daily exercise (not in the evening) 
 Avoid large meals in the evening 
 Ensure exposure to natural light in the daytime 
 Reduce/ stop daytime napping 
 Reduce alcohol intake 
 Reduce stimulant (caffeine and nicotine) intake 
 Associate the bed with sleep. Avoid using the bed to watch TV, listen to the radio, or read 
 Use anxiety management and relaxation techniques 
 Develop a regular routine of rising and retiring at the same time each day (regardless of the amount of sleep taken)

Which of the following is not recommended by the Maudsley Guidelines as a treatment option to augment the 
effect of clozapine? 
 
Olanzapine 
 
Risperidone 
 
Lamotrigine 
 
Haloperidol 
 
Omega-3-triglycerides 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Olanzapine 
Clozapine (resistant schizophrenia) 
Treatment resistant schizophrenia has been estimated to be around 20%.  
Before concluding that a patient is clozapine resistant several factors need to be considered. 
 
Adequate duration of treatment. A substantial proportion of patients have a delayed response. 30% are expected to respond 
within 6 weeks, a further 20% by 3 months, and a further 20% by six months. 
 
Dosage. Plasma levels correlate poorly with clinical response. It is accepted however that a plasma level of 350-450ng/ml must be 
achieved before a patient can be considered resistant. As clozapine undergoes significant metabolism by the P450 enzymes, the 
effects of other medications and smoking need to be considered. 
 
Augmentation 
Should an adequate trial of clozapine fail to be of benefit, augmentation with additional antipsychotics or anti epileptics should be 
considered. 
Sulpride and amisulpride are the favoured antipsychotics for augmentation with clozapine as their selectivity for D2 dopamine 
blockade compliments clozapine (which lacks high potency dopamine blockade). 
Lamotrigine has the best evidence of the mood stabilisers to support its use as an augmentation strategy. 
 
The Maudsley guidelines list the following options for clozapine augmentation:- 
 Amisulpride 
 Aripiprazole 
 Haloperidol 
 Lamotrigine 
 Omega-3-triglycerides 
 Risperidone 
 Sulpiride 
 Topiramate 
 Ziprasidone 
They specifically suggest avoiding using the following:- 
 Pimozide 
 Olanzapine

questions.question_text: It is inversely related to social class, and is therefore more common in those with low education and limited incomes. Somatoform and Dissociative disorders Somatoform disorders The somatoform disorders are a group of disorders characterised by physical symptoms that are presumed to have a psychiatric origin. They are classified slightly differently by the ICD-10 and DSM-IV, see below Categories of somatoform disorders in the ICD-10 Somatisation disorder Undifferentiated somatoform disorder Hypochondriacal disorder Somatoform autonomic dysfunction Persistent somatoform pain disorder Other somatoform disorder Somatoform disorder unspecified Categories of somatoform disorders in the DSM-IV Somatisation disorder Categories of somatoform disorders in the DSM-IV Conversion disorder Hypochondriasis Body dysmorphic disorder Pain disorder Undifferentiated somatoform disorder Somatoform disorder not otherwise specified Questions on these are common. Usually they test a candidate's ability to differentiate between the different types of somatoform disorder. Somatisation disorder (Briquet's syndrome) is characterised by multiple physical complaints affecting many organ systems that cannot be explained by physical disorders. It is more common in women, and normally begins before the age of 30. It is inversely related to social class, and is therefore more common in those with low education and limited incomes. Conversion disorder (referred to as dissociative disorders in the ICD-10) is characterised by a neurological complaint that is related to stress or conflict. It is more common in women and is uncommon in the elderly. It usually presents with weakness, paralysis, pseudoseizures, involuntary movements and sensory disturbances (e.g. Blindness). It is classically associated with the term La belle indifference which refers to the absence of distress despite the presence of a distressing symptom. Hypochondriasis is characterized by a patient's insistence that they suffer with a particular disease, despite evidence to the contrary. Body dysmorphic disorder is characterized by the false belief or exaggerated perception that a part of the body is in some way defective. The most common area perceived to be affected is the skin, followed by the hair, nose, toes, and then weight. Somatoform autonomic dysfunction includes:-  Da Costa's syndrome  Cardiac neurosis  Neurocirculatory asthenia  Dyspepsia  Pylorospasm  Irritable bowel syndrome  Psychogenic flatulence  Psychogenic cough  Hyperventilation  Psychogenic frequency  Dysuria Do not confuse the above with factitious disorder. In factitious disorder a patient will intentionally (deliberately) feign symptoms. Munchausen syndrome is another name for factitious disorder. Dissociative disorders Dissociative disorders are characterised by the loss of integration between memories, identity, immediate sensations, and control of bodily movements. Previously referred to as 'hysteria' (a term best avoided now), dissociative disorders usually occur suddenly in response to a trauma or other intolerable situation. They tend to remit spontaneously after a few weeks to months. A diagnosis requires (ICD-10):  Loss of integration (partial or complete) between memories, identity, sensations and control of bodily movements  No evidence of a physical cause to explain the symptoms  Evidence for psychological causation (if none then the diagnosis should remain provisional) Subtypes include:  Dissociative amnesia  Dissociative fugue  Dissociative stupor  Trance and possession disorders  Dissociative disorders of movement and sensation  Dissociative motor disorders  Dissociative convulsions (pseudoseizures)  Dissociative anaesthesia and sensory loss  Mixed dissociative disorders  Other dissociative disorders (includes Gansers syndrome and multiple personality disorder) Which of the following has consistently been found to be the most prevalent among major epidemiological studies?
questions.explanation:
Anxiety disorders have been found to be the most prevalent in the ECA, NCS-R, NPMS, and the WMH survey initiative. 
Anxiety (epidemiology) 
Anxiety disorders are consistently found to be the most prevalent disorders. This has been demonstrated in the ECA, NCS-R, 
NPMS, and WMH survey initiative. These surveys found that between 10 and 20% of people have had anxiety disorders in the past 
12 months.  
 
Epidemiological catchment area study (ECA) 
Anxiety was the most common mental disorder. The most common type of anxiety disorder was phobic disorder, followed by OCD, 
then panic. Anxiety disorders were twice as common in women as they were in men. 
 
National psychiatric morbidity survey (NPMS) 
The most common type of anxiety disorder was mixed anxiety and depression, followed by GAD. Prevalence rates in women higher 
in all categories except panic in which they were equal. 
 
National Comorbidity Survey (NCS-R) 
Anxiety disorder formed the most prevalent group. Of this group specific phobia was the most prevalent. 
A young woman experiences a sudden loss of vision after witnessing her boyfriend get knocked down by a car. No 
medical cause can be found to explain this. She is surprisingly unconcerned by her symptoms. Select the most likely 
diagnosis. 
 
Persistent somatoform pain disorder 
 
Hypochondriasis 
 
Somatization disorder 
 
Body dysmorphic disorder 
 
Conversion disorder 
 
CORRECT ANSWER : Conversion disorder 
 
 
The lack of concern about her vision is suggestive of La belle indifference which is a feature of conversion disorder.
